title: Async Patterns in Node.js
subtitle: Callbacks, Promises, async/await, and promisify — from callback hell to clean async code
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Node.js is built on async I/O, but JavaScript is single-threaded. Coordinating multiple async operations — especially when they depend on each other — has evolved through three patterns, each solving limitations of the previous.
whyItExists.solution: Callbacks (Node's original pattern) → Promises (chainable, avoids nesting) → async/await (synchronous-looking syntax over Promises). util.promisify converts callback-style functions to Promises so you can use await with older APIs.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Everywhere in Node.js — file reads, database queries, HTTP calls. Always use async/await for new code unless you have a specific reason for callbacks.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Synchronous code is appropriate for startup (reading config, parsing CLI args) where performance doesn't matter and blocking is acceptable.

explainModes.beginner: async/await is the modern way to handle operations that take time (like reading a file or fetching data). Write `async function myFn()` and inside it use `await somePromise` — the code reads top-to-bottom like synchronous code, but it doesn't block while waiting. Use try/catch for errors.
explainModes.simple: Callback pattern (old): fs.readFile(path, (err, data) => { if(err) throw err; use(data); }). Promise pattern: fetchData().then(data => use(data)).catch(err => handle(err)). async/await (modern): async function run() { try { const data = await fetchData(); use(data); } catch(err) { handle(err); } }. Sequential: await a; await b (b waits for a). Parallel: const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()]).
explainModes.standard: util.promisify: converts Node-style (err, result) callbacks to Promises. const readFile = util.promisify(fs.readFile). Promise.all([p1,p2,p3]): run in parallel, resolves when all done. Promise.allSettled: run all, get results for each (won't reject on partial failure). Promise.race: resolves/rejects with whichever settles first. Promise.any: resolves with first success, rejects if all fail. Async error handling: unhandled promise rejections used to be silent — in Node 15+ they crash the process.
explainModes.technical: async functions always return a Promise. await can only be used in async functions (or top-level in ES modules). Awaiting a non-Promise is fine — it's equivalent to Promise.resolve(value). Common mistake: not awaiting inside loops. `for...of` with await works; forEach doesn't (the callback isn't awaited). Solution: for...of or Promise.all(items.map(async item => await process(item))). Async IIFE: (async () => { ... })() — immediately invoked async function for top-level await in CJS.
explainModes.deepDive: The microtask queue: resolved Promises queue their .then() callbacks as microtasks — higher priority than macrotasks (setTimeout, setImmediate). In the event loop, all microtasks drain before the next I/O callback runs. This means deeply chained .then() calls can prevent I/O handling. Use setImmediate() to yield to I/O when needed. AsyncLocalStorage (node:async_hooks): propagates context across await boundaries — used for request-scoped tracing and logging without passing ctx everywhere. AbortController: cancel fetch/async operations via AbortSignal.

content.text: Use Promise.all() to run independent async operations in parallel. Sequential awaits run one at a time — if each takes 100ms and you have 3 of them, sequential takes 300ms, parallel takes ~100ms.

questions.question: You need to fetch user data and their posts simultaneously, then display both. Which approach is best?
options: const user = await fetchUser(id); const posts = await fetchPosts(id);
Use callbacks with a counter variable
questions.explanation: Promise.all() runs both requests concurrently. If fetchUser takes 200ms and fetchPosts takes 150ms, Promise.all takes ~200ms (the max). Sequential awaits would take 350ms (200+150). The chained .then() version works but is harder to read and also runs sequentially. Promise.all is the standard pattern for concurrent independent operations.

faq.q: What happens if I forget `await` in an async function?
faq.a: The Promise is created and starts executing, but you don't wait for it. If you use the result immediately (e.g., const data = fetchUser(id); console.log(data.name)), data is a Promise object, not the resolved value — you'll get undefined or an error. More dangerously: errors inside unresolved Promises become unhandled rejections. In Node 15+, unhandled rejections crash the process. Always await or .catch() Promises you care about.

examples: await Promise.allSettled(emails.map(sendEmail)) — send all emails, collect failures
const data = await fetch(url).then(r => r.json()) — fetch + parse in one await
